subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the debate today on Bill C-21, aimed at giving the Canadian Government sufficient borrowing authority for the year 1984. It is, of course, not the first time a debate on the subject is being held in the House. It is, in fact, a yearly occurrence, when the Government seeks borrowing authority to be able to meet the needs of Canadians and its various departments.
What I find surprising in these yearly debates, and perhaps even more so this year, are the repetitious arguments of the Official Opposition. Every year, we hear the same old cliche about blank cheques and an incredible amount of rhetoric that would have Canadians believe that the Government is doing an incredibly bad job. In fact, their arguments are entirely at odds with what is actually happening in Canada. Mr. Speaker, Canada is a vast and beautiful country, and in this country, in nine provinces out of ten, the authority responsible for collecting taxes from all Canadians or money in any other form, to meet the needs of the provinces, is the Government of Canada. All the more incredible, when one listens to what the Opposition has to say, and surprising, Mr. Speaker, since, as we know there is not a single Liberal government in our Canadian provinces.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Your time will come!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
There are several Conservative governments that spend money and pass legislation to meet the needs of their people. What kind of legislation are they passing and how do they do it? I do not know whether all the provinces are doing a good job, but if we look at Quebec ... It would take a long time to enumerate the many points on which I disagree with the Government of my unfortunate province, which is
increasingly suffering the consequences of having elected an outrageously dominating Parti Quebecois Government. I would not go so far as to say the same of the other provinces, but the fact remains that these are the people, and many are Conservatives like those here in the House, or Members of the New Democratic Party, these are the people who are going to spend a large part of the $29 billion the Canadian Government is seeking to borrow. Mr. Speaker, this year the Canadian government will be giving nearly $20 billion to the provinces in transfer payments to meet the needs of Canadian in areas under provincial jurisdiction, such as health care. I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) who is in the midst of negotiations at the present time and has introduced a Bill to ensure that Canadians receive proper care, that they can be born, live and die in this country with the assurance that Canada can provide them with health care and also post-secondary and technical institutions. Every year, the Government of Canada transfers $20 billion to the provinces. I would therefore suggest that Members of the Opposition who want to know what this money will be used for call up their provincial colleagues who might be able to tell them how that money is going to be spent. I would be surprised if they did because that party is totally inconsistent in several areas. Whether the issue is languages, oil or anything else, what the big brothers in the federal Parliament want, is unwanted by the kid brothers in the provincial Assemblies. In other words, there is no agreement, just controversy. This is more or less how we see the Progressive Conservative party at this time with their nine days' wonder, their new leader who, by the way, now has to cope with a new trend known as "Bring Back Joe", which is gaining quite a momentum in Western Canada, and who does not seem too sure of making it to the upcoming elections.
"Bring back Joe" is the new trend originating from Western Canada. It is the BBJ or "Bring Back Joe" trend, and 1 can easily understand why the Members opposite feel dejected because, as the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) said during the Progressive Conservative leadership campaign a year ago, the Leader of the Opposition is proving to be with every passing day nothing more than just an idolized fake. He even lost the power of speech recently. He found it this afternoon for two short questions and quickly left the House to ask his friend from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) whether he had asked the right questions. I think that he will be back on his usual pedestal tomorrow. Then once again he will lose the power of speech as has been the case these last few weeks.
To come back to the issue being considered, Mr. Speaker, I have heard during the last few days Members opposite trying to make us believe that Canada was getting deep into debt. How awful! Canada is engulfed in debt. I heard the Hon. Member for Joliette yesterday giving as a perfect example the
March 8, 1984

way people use credit cards. Mr. Speaker, what is wrong with using a credit card to pay for what you buy? It is simply a banking tool that was the best example the Hon. Member had to explain what is going on in Canada, but he did not do so. It is obvious that if the credit card user has no money to pay for what he buys with his card and has to borrow from someone else there is a problem. However, when the card user has the money in the bank to pay for his purchases, there is no problem at all in using a credit card.
The Canadian Government will borrow in Canada over 90 per cent of the $29 billion requested in this Bill. This means that Canada will not be borrowing money on the foreign markets. What the Government is asking is the authority to borrow, to obtain the moneys it needs by a means other than taxation to generate economic activity, to fulfill the requirements of the population, to meet its commitments under the various pieces of legislation which were passed through the years in this House by the various parties.
When the Canadian Government borrows from Canadians, is Canada's deficit increasing? No. The deficit of Canada as a nation does not increase. When the Government borrows from Canadians, it uses their money to invest in various social and economic programs, and in most cases, especially in the last few years, the Canadian Government has invested to acquire assets. For instance, in my area of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, the Canadian Government is investing $245 million in infrastructures which will be owned by Canadians to bring gas by way of a pipeline to the area, and this will enable businesses and individuals in the area to buy less crude oil, which often comes from abroad, especially from the Middle East. Such is the cause of the actual deficit, when we have to buy something outside Canada. What the Government is doing is taking money and converting it into an asset, and the best part of it all is that Canadians are the ones who are working to build this pipeline.
The same applies to the other infrastructures which the Government is building for harbours, airports, industries, industrial parks, and so on, in my own area and everywhere else in Canada. Over the past two or three years, the Government has shown its determination to take every advantage of the strong economic recovery and use the money of Canadian taxpayers to set up the mechanisms which, in coming years, will be needed to spur and upgrade our industry to meet the challenge of the new computer technology. It is extremely important that we take that step into the future. Needless to say, the economy has been rather sluggish in the first two years of the current decade. In 1982 and 1983, Mr. Speaker, individual Canadians and businessmen alike have put a lot of money in the bank and been rather reluctant to borrow. But they made an about turn in 1983 as a result of improved economic conditions both in Canada and in the United States, and the Canadian Government also played a major role by
Borrowing Authority Act
offering incentives such as the $3,000 home construction grants and other incentives.
The result of all this, Mr. Speaker, was that a lot of people ended up with huge bank accounts, as many of our fellow Canadians did.
Would Hon. Members of the Opposition have preferred that Canadian banks lend that money to foreigners, for instance? Do they think that when a Canadian puts money in the bank and earns interest on his deposit that the interest falls from heaven? When a deposit brings in interest, it is because the borrower has put the money to work or because the bank which took the deposit has loaned the money to somebody.
Let us say that the Government stops borrowing, as the Opposition seems to be suggesting. Who will go out tomorrow and borrow the $29 billion needed to stimulate the economy? If the Government, as leader of the country and the main lever behind economic activities, does not show that it is prepared to promote economic growth actively to fight unemployment, who among businessmen will have enough confidence to get his feet wet if the Government itself is standing still? Will we let the major Canadian banks lend money to Third World countries or even to Eastern nations whose regime is so corrupt that they cannot even repay the interest on their debts? Is that what the Opposition parties want? We do not know, Mr. Speaker. It never fails, it is always the same old tune!
It is unbelievable, but I see across the floor people who have been elected years ago and who are supposedly knowledgeable in economic affairs, yet they keep repeating the same irrelevant and misleading speeches, trying to make Canadians believe that they will end up in bread lines if the Government keeps borrowing, that it is increasing the national debt when it borrows from Canadians. That is not true. Mr. Speaker, some countries have found themselves in financial straits because they borrowed too much on foreign money markets. That has been the economic bane of a number of countries, but Canada is certainly not among them. What the Canadian Government is doing now and what it has done in recent years is that it has assumed that responsibility when Canadians were reluctant to invest as they used to, it has made the investments required to get our economy moving.
Yesterday I heard the Hon. Member for Simcoe South or Simcoe North tell the House that the Bank of Canada rate was going to increase as a result of Canada's huge $30 billion deficit-

pressure on interest rates in Canada . . . This is something they kept saying everywhere when they were in office in 1979. The strongest pressure on interest rates in Canada comes from the interest rates of American banks. Whatever the level of borrowing of the Canadian Government, it changes absolutely nothing. Because tomorrow morning, even if Canada's operating deficit were nil our interest rates would have to be comparable to those in the United States to support our dollar.
And why at this point should we tell Canadians that the borrowing level of the Canadian Government has an impact on interest rates, when we know full well they reflect what goes on down South? Again, this is presumably political tactics of the kind that was used in Manitoba by their provincial colleagues, to make Manitobans believe that if Francophones were given rights everyone would lose his shirt, his bones or his job, everyone would have to be bilingual in that province. No. That kind of tactics, Mr. Speaker, tends to upset the people needlessly.
In all fairness, if those Opposition parties were serious, they would try to work out or help us work out policies that would be good for Canadians. This is what the Canadian Government has been trying to do and has been doing for years. An area such as mine, a so-called resource area, which has been a major source of electrical power for the rest of Canada and the people down South since the turn of the century an area which is an extremely important source of wood, pulp and paper, aluminum, and various resources is one where work is often seasonal. In my constituency, many people work only six months a year. This is part of our life pattern, because there are operations at the resource level that are conducted on a seasonal basis only. Should this country penalize people because they are in the Saguenay-Lake St. Jean area rather than in Montreal? Should Canada forget to support the people in areas such as mine when there are no jobs available? If the Canadian Government were to do that it means it would have to pay to set up infrastructures that would be used only six months a year to bring workers to large centres, which would create big social problems! That is not the way the Liberal Party of Canada under Pierre Elliott Trudeau and his supporters have envisioned this country over the years. His vision of this country was one where people were given the opportunity to move about, to settle down to grow, to develop, and to live all year-round, whichever they please, through economic policies established by the Canadian government such as DREE or the new DREE or the PRID Program intensive economic development policies, whether it be through job creation programs or manpower training in plants or in schools, or the various policies for direct social action, which I referred to earlier, such as medicare and support to university, technical and college training programs. All Canadians-men and women-were given the right to be born, to live, to receive health care to retire, to work, as I said earlier, to exist. One of the struggles we have just won is that pregnant women are no longer penalized by the Employment Insurance Act for giving
Canada the gift of life which will produce the next generation of Canadians means today-
This is what being Canadian to be able to be born, to live, to be cared for, to be housed, to be fed, to grow up, to retire carefree and at all time, to enjoy freedom of action, freedom of speech, freedom of thought. But all this, Mr. Speaker, requires money. And what the Canadian Government is doing, whether the Official Opposition likes it or not, is to borrow from Canadians to invest in Canada and to give work and benefits to Canadians. In the final analysis, Canadians receive interests on the money they have lent to a country they trust, to their own country, to their Government, to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of straightforward questions to put to the Hon. Member. I listened to his speech and found it very interesting. He is obviously very concerned about the ability of the Canadian economy to recover and to get back to life, in a sense. He has indicated a number of steps that the Government has taken in that direction.
My questions are restricted to a particular area. At a time when we need consumer spending as one of the factors which will kick-start our economy back to life or sustain a recovery, could the Hon. Member explain how the Government's increasing of taxes to the average Canadian family of somewhere between $200 and $300 per family would assist the recovery at a time when disposable incomes are needed to allow Canadians to purchase additional goods and services? Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's question surprises me somewhat. If the Government is now requesting a borrowing authority of $30 billion, it is because during recent years, it has decided to give more discretionary money to all Canadians. I do not know how he can refer to a tax increase of $200 or $300. He is probably considering more than one tax.
I do not deny the fact that some taxes can fluctuate but generally, it cannot be said that Canadians are now paying more federal taxes than at the beginning of the '70's. Quite the contrary. Federal taxes have always been indexed, as we all know, and if we consider the increased revenues during the last ten or fifteen years, compared to what Canadian taxpayers are paying to their Government, it is quite the contrary. I will even go further. In the last budget, it is provided that the individuals who spend their entire income, for example those who receive the guaranteed income supplement, will get an additional $50 at the end of the year 1984 from the Canadian Government. They are the best consumers in Canada, because they spend their entire income.
March 8, 1984

The same applies to statutory increases granted under the various welfare programs of the Government for senior citizens or for the unemployed. The unemployment insurance system, which is a comprehensive insurance provided by the Canadian Government is also indexed every year. The economy will benefit from these consumers who, as I said, are our best consumers, because whether they are unemployed or not, the money they receive from the Government of Canada is almost immediately reinvested in the Canadian economy.
In a town such as my home-town of Alma, whose industrial infrastructure over the past six or seven years has been quite unstable as a result of the modernization or closing of plants which were no longer competitive, a million dollars in unemployment insurance benefits are injected every week. Otherwise, our tradesmen who are helping hundreds and even thousands of unemployed workers survive would have much difficulty supporting them in their hour of need. It will be my responsibility, as a Member of Parliament, to make sure that until such a time as the provincial government comes to our rescue by providing us with aluminium works or some other plant to restore the Alma area to the strong economic position it enjoyed previously, we have many more Canada Works projects, unemployment insurance policies and schemes for the redistribution of wealth throughout Canada, so that although our plants may not be producing it year round we can still continue to provide the South with aluminium, and survive the rest of the year.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-21, an Act to provide borrowing authority, it seems to me that I would be remiss if I did not suggest that this whole process can be repetitious and unnecessary. It suggests that we have to look again for major overhauls and streamlining in parliamentary reform.
The process we go through, in budgets and finance at least, Mr. Speaker, reminds me of the explanation a clergyman gave as to what he did when he gave a sermon to his congregation. He said, "First I tell them what I am going to tell them, then I tell them what I am telling them, and then I tell them what I told them." It seems to me that this applies to the whole budgetary process. First, we tell them what we are going to do. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) brings in a Budget. Overall Estimates are given by Departments for what needs to be done. Huge piles of information are provided as to what will be spent. Documentation which we get when the Budget is brought down can literally be six or seven inches high. Then we explain not only what will be spent, but also what we will receive in terms of revenues in our Budget papers. Then we talk about what the shortfall, which is called the deficit, will be. Finally we discuss what must be borrowed. All that is in the budgetary process. We debate the Budget for eight days, giving quite a bit of time to all of these facts. That is telling them what we are going to do.
Then we tell them what we are doing. That process goes on at length. We submit the Estimates in detail as to how much each Department will spend. These Estimates, as they are called, comprise what the Government submits are going to be the amounts of money needed to conduct the Government's business. We take into account the fact that aside from the money the Government collects in income tax for the provinces, a very large part of the federal Budget, that section which is given for federal taxation, is also transferred to the provinces. In fact, estimates have been made, Mr. Speaker, that approximately 60 per cent is now either collected by the provinces or transferred to the provinces in what is collected through income taxes. In other words, we then say how much we will have to spend. The Government again submits huge piles of material to give a detailed accounting of what was spent last year and what the Estimates are for this year. They are debated, sent to committee, witnesses are called, there is ample opportunity to discuss and debate them some more, and then they are finally passed.
Then we continue to tell them what we are telling them. We have Budget Bills. We may have one, two, three or more Budget Bills. These are there to implement the raising of the money and to authorize the taxes. Each of these, Mr. Speaker, is debated, discussed, passed through various phases, sent to committee perhaps, and then finally they come back and are passed.
You would think that after all this debate on the Budget, the Estimates and the Bills for executing the Budget, we would then have exhausted the subject. But no, we must still have another Bill. We now have to tell them again what we told them. This one is to authorize the Government to borrow the money needed to do what Parliament has already agreed needs to be done.
That is what we are doing now, Mr. Speaker. We are debating the Bill to borrow the money which the Budget has predicted will be needed, that is, $29,550 billion, which includes a $4 billion cushion to meet possible unexpected contingencies. It seems to me that there is a little too much repetition. Think of the time which could be saved if the parliamentary system were streamlined and planned in order to eliminate at least one of these operations. However, such is the system we have. Even though we have already justified the expenses and revenues, and therefore the deficit and borrowing needs in the Budget, we now come back to hear the same repetition and litany of gloom and doom from the Opposition Members. But there are many others who are not as pessimistic as they are. Last night, when I attended a meeting of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, I was impressed by the fact that they did not bring to Ottawa a long list of grievances, pejorative attacks and a crying towel. To the contrary, they came to express a feeling of relief that a real process of consultation has been developing over the last several years between business, labour and government. They pointed out that this dialogue which the Minister of Finance has initiated led to real results and improvements in creating a positive climate for business over the last two budgets. It is a positive
March 8, 1984

climate for businesses, large and small, to develop an ability to improve their productivity, profits and competitiveness. They also felt that this dialogue must continue.
They pointed out that we in the country are not yet back to where we were before the recession. They also noted last night that the recovery was real and the future, if this dialogue between government and business will continue, was more promising.
We in the Government share their concerns, lest the deficit become a chronic case, lest interest rates and inflation rise and the recovery be nipped in the bud. But what was significant was their anticipation of better results from dialogue and co-operation.
Business leaders to whom I spoke last night and to whom I have been speaking generally have expressed those thoughts in the last couple of years. They also asked me last night what I thought. I explained that we believe the deficit which we have budgeted is necessary to keep the economy growing and fuelled, to honour the commitments to social justice we have made, as well as to provide useful employment. I pointed out that our deficit is not as serious in its implications as is the American deficit, as the Americans themselves have pointed out, because ours is not the same kind of structural deficit and therefore not as dangerous as the one in the United States.
If we get the economy stoked up to a sufficient level, more people will go to work and therefore will be able to pay their taxes. In turn, we will be able to receive revenues, which again will increase the amount of employment and reduce the deficit. If the money we borrow is spent to provide jobs, those who will be earning money will no longer need the social safety nets which cost the Government money. The system will prove beneficial because when they return to work the deficit will be reduced.
I also observed that our deficit is a lower percentage of our GNP. This is something that the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) just indicated. Our deficit today is a lower percentage of our gross national product than it was some 30 years ago in the days of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. My reason for pointing this out was not to minimize the seriousness of deficits but to put them in perspective. When we have a deficit, we must borrow. That is the reason for this borrowing Bill. But the reason why we are budgeting and planning a deficit is that we are investing in Canadians and in the future of Canada. If a government of Canada does not believe in Canada, then we cannot expect other Canadians to believe in Canada. In other words, we are not just borrowing to give handouts. We are borrowing to make the new Budget possible, and the new Budget will invest in making the climate better for large and small businesses, farmers and fishermen to enable them to become the engine for industry to work and the economy to roll.
Of course, making the climate for businesses better will cost the Government money. It will increase our deficit. But we are assured in our dialogue with businessmen that the gains that
Borrowing Authority Act
we make in improving the climate for businesses will be so great that they will fuel a recovery which will more than compensate for the revenue that is lost. For example, some of the deficits in our new Budget will go to creating a better tax system, a system which will stimulate and reward investment in business. The new Budget will simplify the tax reporting system and the bookkeeping for over 300,000 small businesses, which will give them the incentive to continue to increase investment in their own companies and motivate them to continue to be in business. While that will cost the Government revenue, it will provide relief for the small businessman and provide him with incentives to invest further.
The new Budget will improve the fairness of the tax system. It will give farmers the long hoped for break in transferring their farms to the next generation, and it will also ensure that they will have an opportunity to work incrementally on the side in other kinds of work in order to keep their farms operating and to survive without being penalized. They will be able to write off the losses of their farm operations.
Again, the new Budget will provide aid to the private sector to play a larger role in international development. It will aid the Canadian automobile industry by ensuring that it has a fairer opportunity to compete with foreign auto makers in the Canadian marketplace.
The budget will aid the petroleum industry and much more. All of these programs will cost money. This will increase the deficit. However, we believe, as a result of our dialogue with businessesmen, that they have convinced us that if we take certain measures which will cost us only a relatively small amount of money, the returns from the infusion of enthusiasm and elimination of much paperwork will give those companies new opportunities to grow and be encouraged. For example, this will be done through our efforts in making rather large investments in aid overseas through aid in trade. It will also provide Canadian businesses with new opportunities that otherwise would not be there. In order to help business we must bring up a deficit at this point. Of course, that deficit requires us to borrow money, and that is the purpose of our debate today.
The Opposition questions us about all the money we are wasting. If we were wasting money, I would be against it. When evidence is brought to light which indicates that this happens, I certainly am the first to call for a halt. On the other hand, it is the opinion of some Members that the money we spend on some programs is wasteful. Some in the Opposition do not favour the growth of social services and social spending, but I must ask if raising the guaranteed income supplement to bring single pensioners over the poverty line is wasting money. I do not think so, and I hope that not too many Members of the House hold that view. I believe that giving money to pensioners who built this country and are now elderly Canadians, but whose present pensions have been eroded before their eyes because of inflation, is paying an old debt. They are in a situation where they are no longer able to live in dignity, and it seems to me that we are simply paying an old debt. If we must borrow to pay that debt it should be our first priority.

March 8, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
Furthermore, it is not like buying oil overseas when money is being sent away, because giving pensions to elderly Canadians means that Canadians are paying Canadians. The money that those senior citizens receive is not being put away in a bank; it is money that will be spent immediately and put back into the system. People at this level of income, such as GIS recipients, will certainly be putting that money back into the Canadian economy immediately through the purchase of goods and services and professional assistance. This, in turn, will put Canadians to work who will then be able to pay taxes. Those revenues will ultimately lead to a reduction in the deficit. Therefore, the money paid in pensions will be circulated throughout the country, and some of it will come back to the federal government in the form of taxes that are paid by those who serve pensioners.
Is putting billions of dollars into employment wasting money? That is one of the many reasons we incur a deficit and borrow. We are putting billions of dollars into employment. We believe retraining Canadians for more relevant jobs is a good investment. We believe that putting money into educational programs, job retraining, career planning and job searching is an investment into our human resources. This will pay off because it will enable our people to do the kind of work and to provide the services that can be carried in goods and trade to other countries. People will be more capable and more productive if they are retrained and re-educated. They will be able to hold jobs that are more productive. This in turn will make Canadian products more competitive abroad.
Sure, it causes a deficit if you put money into that kind of retraining and education. But so does borrowing for improving plant facilities. Businessmen know that they have to renew their plants, buy new machinery and keep up with modern technology to be competitive. Therefore, they are prepared to invest in their resources and their plants. We, on the other hand, have to be prepared to invest in human resources, the engine to make plants work using modern technology. While it may seem a great expenditure of money, it is money that is worth borrowing and worth spending. We are investing in the best and most important thing we can, the people of our country. That is what our Government is doing.
I could go on to discuss all the steps we have taken to invest in Canada, Mr. Speaker. You could look at the renewal of railway lines in the West, the double-tracking and the building of tunnels. Yes, the Government is putting in billions of dollars, but then more and more billions of dollars are being put in by private enterprise, not only to match but to double and triple that investment. This will provide the kind of swift transportation needed to carry the products of the people of central Canada to the West Coast and will provide an outlet for Canadian goods to get to the ports and then on to the marketplace in the Pacific Rim.
While we invest in the railroads, this investment brings people to work. Canadians can then sell their wheat, their potash, and other products, thus earning money for Canada,
which will produce taxes and reduce the deficit. That is an investment in the future. I could give examples of other investments in our infrastructure-the building of roads, communications systems, and so on-which will make us more effective and more competitive. This will bring more sales for Canadian goods and trade. Most of the spending which causes deficits puts Canadians to work. People then pay taxes which reduce the deficit.
We believe in Canada, Mr. Speaker. We want Canadians to believe in Canada. The world sees us as a shining example. Others believe in Canada more than Canadians believe in Canada. We hear carping and negative voices amplified by the purveyors of news who usually think that the only good news is bad news. They talk of gloom and doom. We borrow because we believe in Canadians, we believe in Canada, and we believe in our future.

Borrowing Authority Act
fulfill the commitments that it places on the Supplementary and Main Estimates. It stands to reason that any lay persons, regardless of whether they have been in business or not, with the kinds of statements coming from the Government side that affect us, would believe it is all right to have increased deficits year after year, accumulating to the point where it takes almost our national savings, public or private to pay the national debt.
It is not logical to assume that you can run a government any different from a business. It is grossly unfair to leave the impression that we are just borrowing from ourselves, that it is totally okay for A to borrow from B because we are all in the same nation. That is like saying it is all right for Eaton's to borrow from Simpson's or The Bay to borrow from some other retail establishment. If their debts keep going up and up, sooner or later the day of reckoning will come. It will not come during your or my term of office. The day of reckoning will come when our children and grandchildren cannot borrow any more just to service the debt.
We are now looking at a debt in Canada that exceeds the total budget of the Canadian Government of not very many years ago. I am getting a little tired of listening to Members on the Government side saying that it does not matter how much we borrow, that we can borrow all we need plus. They expect the NDP and Conservative Opposition to hold up their hands and say there is nothing wrong borrowing more than you need. There is. We are not going to trust the Government with a $4 billion extra amount this time around. We are asking for a $10 billion reduction in the $29.5 billion for which it is asking. The Government is irresponsible. It is not accountable to the Canadian people if it believes it is going to hoodwink everyone in Canada into believing that a $4 billion slush fund is okay. safe to say that anyone who commits first degree murder today will be locked up for 25 years, and anyone who commits second degree murder will be locked up for 15 years with no chance of parole before the sentence is served.

Why do we have political lobbies? An Hon. Member opposite mentioned the pro-life movement. If I happen to be a pro-life supporter and my constituents lobby me long and hard enough, they might convince me that there is a need to study the issue of abortion-not to reinstate it-and I would be prepared to study it in committee.
Who in the House would not be prepared to study the most recent statistics dealing with criminal acts of violence resulting in murder? I suggest that a lot of people on the other side of the House would not be too willing to have that reviewed in committee. I think there is a good deal of piloting on this issue by some leaders on the other side of the House. Why else would they vote against referring the matter to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs?
I brought the same issue before the House on the only day we had a vote on capital punishment, to my knowledge, since 1979. There was an all-Party vote not three years ago on a motion that I presented to the House. It did not deal with a return to capital punishment but was a simple request for the subject matter to be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The purpose was to review the most recent statistics; to determine in our minds, as the responsible Members of Parliament we think we are, just where we are going on the issue. There is not only our own position to consider but also the position of the people who sent us here. There are only three ways you can vote, Mr. Speaker-with your Party, with your conscience, or with your constituents. There is no other way to go.
In this Private Member's Bill I am asking that consideration be given to referring the subject matter of the Bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. In that way we could review the most recent statistics and determine in our own minds whether someone who stabs an 18 year old boy to death in Mississauga should be eligible for parole in 25 years; whether someone who shoots a girl in a Becker's store in Mississauga and paralyses her for life-not 25 years, but life-should be eligible for parole, in 15 years, and whether a man who stabs a man fatally after raping his wife or girl friend should get more than a slap on the wrist and five years in jail.
Things change, Mr. Speaker. Circumstances change, society changes and society needs protection in some of these areas. We cannot just pass a Bill and hope that the whole thing will go away. There is a lot of unrest in the country about what is happening to law enforcement today and about whether the sentence fits the crime.
It can be asked how someone can be a pro-life supporter and, at the same time, support capital punishment. That is a difficult question to answer. It took me a long time to solve that problem in my own mind. When I am dealing with the pro-life issue versus abortion, 1 am dealing with an innocent person, the unborn child. For that reason I have a great deal of difficulty supporting abortion under any circumstances. But when I am talking about capital punishment and the way to treat an individual who stabbed, shot and murdered, I am dealing with a person proven to be guilty by the courts. 1 would be the first to admit that the courts are not always right and that you cannot bring life back once it is taken. At the same time, however, you cannot say to the people adversely affected by the act that it is fair to let the perpetrator free to go out and do it a second time.
If government does not satisfy society's need for protection with a sentence to fit the crime, then it is irresponsible. That applies to all of us.
Bills that go from second reading to committee do not always return to the House in the same form, Mr. Speaker. It is very easy for anyone to find something in the bill that he or she does not like. Perhaps they do not want to see a person hanged but would sooner see them electrocuted, injected or have any number of things happen to them. That is not what we are discussing at the moment; all we are discussing is whether the issue deserves consideration in committee.
I hope that at the conclusion of today's debate there will be an indication from Members of the Government that the issue can be reviewed in committee. We could hear witnesses and listen to some of the associations that are interested, such as the police associations and law enforcement agencies, and people who have been affected by a murder in the family. We could review the subject matter and perhaps make another decision for a free vote. I hope serious consideration will be given to the matter of how to deal satisfactorily with people who commit premeditated first degree murder.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REINSTATE CAPITAL PUNISHMENT FOR CERTAIN CRIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue raised by the Private Member's Bill is a very serious one. It is one that keeps coming back to the House through the efforts of Members and, from time to time, of the public. It is a difficult question to handle, and I believe the Hon. Member would ultimately like it to go through the next stage and eventually end up as a free vote, because that is where it would end up somewhere down the line. There is an attractive thought to that, to review a process which has already been reviewed and on which in fact we had a free vote in 1976. The result at that time, Mr. Speaker, as we know, is that Parliament passed into law a Bill which officially brought capital punishment to an end. However, the death penalty was replaced by a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment with a
March 8, 1984

minimum parole eligibility period of 25 years for first degree murder and a 10 year to 15 year minimum eligibility period for second degree murder.
It would appear from this motion which has been brought forward before the House today, and the many motions which have come before us over the years, that in fact the 1976 vote did not forever settle the matter. In fact, since then we have had a stream of Private Members' Bills, motions and proposals for a national referendum on the subject, another look at the whole situation and, perhaps, another free vote in the House.
1 suppose we have to take opportunities like this. I do not think there is anything wrong with it. It is a very serious moral question in the country, as the Hon. Member has said. It is also a subject which each of us as an individual will have to work out in his own mind, whether we do it in the formal setting, as has been suggested, or as we contemplate the lurid crimes which take place in many of our communities across the land. I suppose we would then, Mr. Speaker, have to dwell a little bit on the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent. The Hon. Member opposite is quite right to bring this matter before us again for perusal, whether it be in committee, as was suggested, or in this forum. However, the statistics which I have seen on the subject so far do not seem to indicate that there has been an increase in capital crime since the law was changed. I have not looked at these statistics within the last couple of weeks, but if memory serves me correctly, I think in fact there has been a decrease in capital crime.
It is a moral question with which we must deal, and I suppose it will continue to come up in light of the cold-blooded crimes which have been committed very recently, and they have been mentioned before. We have had in my riding comparable crimes, very sporadically, thank the Lord, but they do happen. Therefore, when one looks at those cold-blooded crimes, it seems to be a very appropriate solution to take the position of an eye for an eye. However, one must take a look at the other side of the coin, I feel, and try to maintain a cool perspective on the whole situation. The question is whether the state has the right deliberately to take a human life. The right to life is given explicit recognition, I remind each of us, in our new Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I do not believe we can simply accept the principle of an eye for an eye. There are other areas where the state, in punishing people for crimes committed, does not work on an eye-for-an-eye principle, and that is what taking another life by the state is all about. If we work on that principle, we could perhaps drift back to the extreme example of societies where if one mutilates another individual, he will be mutilated in return, and so on. I feel the suggestion of capital punishment is that it suits the crime because the person has taken someone else's life, and if we extend that theory, then that presents a pretty monstrous thought of how we might deal with a number of possible situations.
Capital Punishment
We are dealing with a very moral question and a difficult one to resolve, and I come back to the question: Does the state have the right to take someone else's life deliberately? Would a return to capital punishment be in fact an effective deterrent? Once a crime has been committed, yes, we must appropriately punish the person responsible for the crime, no matter what its nature, but more important, in another sense, we must try to deter future actions in that same area. I do not believe that capital punishment would necessarily act as a greater deterrent. Nothing has been stated so far which would prove that. In fact, I do not believe we are coddling criminals or acting immorally in handing out the kinds of sentences which are being handed out now in relation to mandatory life sentences and matters of that sort.
Once again I come back to the question of the appropriateness of capital punishment. Those who are in favour of it have the burden of proving that this form of execution by the state is justified. It seems that this ultimate penalty carries with it the seeds of severe injustice through its potentially unequal application to the poor, the ignorant, the uneducated, and through the very real possibility that it might be applied in error. This has happened, despite the elaborate safeguards which have been built into the system. No matter how shocking some of the particular examples which are described by anti-abolitionists, it is unlikely that many of those crimes would constitute first degree murder, given the emotional element of the crime and the lack of premeditation.
I believe that, as the Hon. Member has suggested, we have to also consider the feelings of the public at large. We are in this House, after all, representatives of the constituencies, the constituency of Canada and the constituency of our individual ridings. While it is attractive to take a look at capital punishment as the ultimate solution to a problem, I am not aware of any overwhelming change in public opinion which says we must return to capital punishment. I do not believe Gallup polls of which I am aware would support that idea.
While I personally have had some representations in my riding on the subject, as I suppose all Hon. Members have had from time to time, particularly when some abhorrent crime takes place within our area-and perhaps participating in this kind of a discussion will precipitate it-I am not aware, nor have I had any strong representations from my constituents at large telling me that they would like to see this matter reopened, re-explored and perhaps once more go back to the House for a free vote. There are many things within our system, Mr. Speaker, with which we are not comfortable, which we do not like, which we as Members of Parliament must deal with. We must deal with tax matters, and everyone would rather not talk about that. However, we must act as parliamentarians and do the necessary things to make sure that the country has the revenue it needs to carry on the programs deemed necessary.
The problem is, as I said earlier, a moral one. Is it right for the state deliberately to take a life? In so doing it might be justified if we had proof positive, or a stronger expression of proof, that by taking the life of a particular abhorrent criminal

March 8, 1984
Capital Punishment
we have done something more than just take revenge, that we have actually done something which would add to the deterrent factor in capital crimes.
While it is argued, I believe, by the Hon. Member opposite that capital punishment would in itself deter capital crime, I cannot agree with that particular argument. I agree that we have to take a firmer stand on capital crimes. We have to become more firm in the sentences passed. But that is another way of dealing with the same problem. I would support capital punishment if it would preclude someone else's life being taken in a particularly abhorrent fashion. I too have wrestled with this issue and I would go that route. However, I am afraid that I personally am not convinced that that is the way to go at this particular time.
This debate is useful in that it reminds us of a subject that we, whether we like it or not, as Members of Parliament have to look at one way or another periodically. That is necessary. When 1 was given the opportunity to participate in today's debate, I did so almost reluctantly because we are opening a can of worms that we really do not want to get into if we can avoid it. However, that is a coward's way out, so I am pleased to have been given this chance to express a few thoughts on the subject.
I know I will probably hear from many people in my constituency on this issue, pro or con. I welcome that because this is a way of developing opinion and a feel for the people we are here to serve. However, I must conclude that so far I have not heard any compelling reason for reopening the debate further than we have done here today. I believe the matter has been given careful attention over time in the House and elsewhere, and I believe this debate will precipitate another careful look at a very difficult issue.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REINSTATE CAPITAL PUNISHMENT FOR CERTAIN CRIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this debate I am not primarily in agreement with the argument that all we want is a discussion. As I understand it, we are asked to give approval to the Bill on second reading, which would mean approval in principle. That I cannot do.
A few years ago Parliament decided to abolish the death penalty. As part of the general public I was very much in agreement and pleased with that decision. I still believe the decision was sound. I want to give my reasons for that, but first I want to consider what I find to be the main arguments in restoring the death penalty.
The most common argument I hear is that it is needed as a deterrent. This is where the extreme examples are most powerfully used. The example of a particularly recent and particularly dreadful murder is bound to move a person. There is also an argument which is a little bit more general, and which I would say really means we want in principle to satisfy our anger. Some people would use rather old fashioned imagery, perhaps even quoting selectively from the Old Testament about justice and retribution. However, I think the moving force there is anger, which I note can arise over one matter but
be expressed on something entirely different. In this case people find their anger is often brought to the surface when they read a newspaper story about a dreadful murder. They say that that guy ought to be hanged, or else they express even more lurid alternatives for what ought to be done to him. They are not angry at that guy. They may not be particularly concerned with the person killed. They may be just angry, angry about something in the family, something at work, on the street, and this is an outlet for the anger.
The third argument is like the second, but there is an attempt to make it much more reasoned. Those people argue that there is a principle of justice involved in which the innocent victim should be distinguished from a guilty killer. If we do not make that distinction, quite apart from anger or deterrence, we are simply being unjust.
On the other side, Mr. Speaker, I find mainly two arguments used in opposing the death penalty. One is that the courts, with the best will and effort in the world, are still subject to error. There have been cases of the wrong person being executed for a crime. There is a case we all know of the wrong person having been imprisoned for a crime. Fortunately he was not executed, although in his case he probably would not have been executed under the previous law. But the case does raise the question.
The other argument is that focusing on the death penalty for carefully defined premeditated murder, while having some merit in the abstract, I think narrows far too much the attention of people to a very limited kind of crime. It narrows it down to the individual who may be frustrated by all kinds of injustices he or she has experienced directly from the person he or she killed or, more generally, from society, as when a person walks into some public office and kills one of the public servants there because of what he thinks is the run-around he has received over life necessities such as workmen's compensation or other public obligations. The two great dangers of using the death penalty are that we may make the ultimate mistake of killing the wrong person. Second, it seems to treat the matter, in a sense, too easily. I know it may seem ridiculous to say that killing a person is treating it easily, but killing one individual may be a way of kidding ourselves into thinking that we have solved the problem of violence in our society to an extent that we simply have not.
That is a brief statement why I think there are strong arguments against the death penalty, and I want to return now to the arguments in favour. The first one I mentioned was that of deterrence. There will be less people killed by murderers if we restore the death penalty. That is an attractive argument and, like many others, if I were convinced that the argument was true I would have a much harder time opposing or voting against the death penalty. But I am not convinced. There are studies, not just in Canada but in many other countries, which show very powerfully that whether there is a death penalty or not, it does not seem to make much difference overall. Undoubtedly there are some cases in which we are told it does. When you add it all together, it does not seem that it is a
March 8, 1984

reliable method worth stacking against the risk of an innocent person being killed by the State.
Further, there is the evidence in our own country that since the death penalty was repealed, not only did the rate of murders per capita not rise, but in fact it declined slightly. 1 have not heard anyone argue that abolishing the death penalty caused a reduction in the rate of murders. I cannot imagine that being a likely argument. However, I cannot find any argument that the abolition of the death penalty caused an increase or was followed by a significant increase. There were ups and downs, but more downs than ups, in the rate of murders per capita. I do not think there is a sustainable argument that the death penalty is an effective deterrent.
I believe anger may be the main motivating factor among people who say "hang him" or "shoot him" or whatever else. It is sometimes justified by words taken out of an historical context from the Old Testament; "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth", anyone that kills shall be killed and so on. That is a law which very few people now take seriously in all its instances in the Old Testament, the scripture of the Jewish people. It is also a law which was specifically superseded in the teaching of the religion to which 1 belong. The teaching there is that law is now superseded and anyone who is angry with another person will be brought before the court of judgement. The teaching says that the distinction between the murder and the anger which may have led to the murder should not be made so hard and fast. We should not think we are free to indulge in anger and in expressing our anger in all kinds of ways, but so long as we stop short of murder we are all right. That is a misunderstanding of the teaching of the Old Testament which was specifically countered by the teaching of the New Testament.
I find from my own experience, and I see around me, that vengeance is a very common desire. I will not say it is natural to people because I am not sure what is natural to people. It certainly is habitual. If somebody hurts me, I want to hurt him. It is often done vicariously. When I hear of somebody in our city, our country, or another country doing something dreadful, I may want to hurt that person. That is not healthy. I say it is habitual. I do not think it is natural to human beings and I do not think it is healthy. I find from personal and public experience that indulging in anger does not satisfy. When I decided to hit back at somebody physically when I was younger, or verbally now that I have grown older, and I do hit back, usually I want to then hit back again and again. It is never enough. I think that is not a unique experience. Anger does not really satisfy. Rather, there is something inherent about it which dissatisfies. Of course, when you kill a person, you cannot kill him again. However, you can go on looking for more people to kill and more excuses to kill them. That is not a healthy habit for society.
There is the third argument about principle and fairness. Why should an innocent person suffer by being murdered and a guilty person suffer less, that is, by not being killed? On this
Capital Punishment
point we have to look again at the remark of Jesus about anger to which I referred before, that anger is like murder. He did not say they are exactly the same but he said we will be judged for either of them. When we are angry at murders we should also remember there are people who are angry at deaths by automobile accidents on the road. There are people who are angry at death by Fire when they are caused by negligence, for example, of an absentee landlord. We have had some terrible fire-trap deaths in downtown Toronto. There is bitter, deep-seated, long-running anger amongst hundreds of thousands of industrial workers in Canada over our country's negligent record of industrial safety. Construction workers, miners and other workers have been required to work under unnecessarily dangerous conditions by employers who sometimes conceal the facts of the danger. An example of this is asbestosis. Governments connived that concealment and therefore caused painful death by cancer of employees in those industries. There is a lot of anger over those deaths. However, no employer or Government inspector is ever brought to court and accused of those deaths in the criminal sense. There is anger over those people being let off scott free with what is not legally defined as murder but, in the minds of many workers in this country, is equivalent to murder. Why not put a negligent employer at least in jail when he knowingly profits by risking the lives of employees because he is too cheap to pay the cost of safety devices and procedures?
We must go a little further with this. This country likes to indulge in violence where it is profitable. The TV industry peddles violence continually. It makes violence attractive to look at, think about and contemplate because there is money in peddling violence. This country allows the TV industry to do it in the same way as this country promotes the consumption of alcohol to excess. We have ads in the streetcars saying, "Don't drink too much, but drink". The question of what is too much, of course, is uncontrollable.
We have the often unnecessary use of firearms for sport. We have the glorification of the way of life of killing, whether in the military or hunting. This country likes to promote a spirit of violence. However, when someone is carried too far by it and kills a person, we then want to use that person as a scapegoat. We want to blot out all the other violence in the country and blame that person for the whole of it as a scapegoat. We want to transfer our sense of guilt to him. It is not healthy, Mr. Speaker. It does not stop murder. All the public hangings in the 19th century did not wipe out murder. Although hangings are not made such lurid festivals any more, the statistics in the 20th century show the same thing. They do not blot out murder.
There is no serious reason for supposing that if this Bill were approved at second reading it would lead to anything that would reduce murder, the occasion of anger or satisfy any principle of justice within our country. I believe it would be far more to the point to pay stronger attention to the care of victims of murder, that is to say, those immediately connected

March 8, 1984
Capital Punishment
to the murder victim. This is an area in wich there is still a great deal of room for positive and constructive action.
I believe there is also a great deal of room for intelligent action on the reduction of social activities that encourage violence, whether it is the careless use of automobiles, the careless use of alcohol, the careless use of firearms or, for that matter, the glorification of physical violence in certain sports. I have played football, rugby and soccer. I have boxed. I have engage in unarmed combat training in the army. I understand something of the enthusiasm for combat. I also understand that it can be very dangerous. I believe that the entire sports enterprise must be much more careful about how body contact sports are promoted. Whenever there is money to be made in those sports, anger and violence is peddled for the sake of earning that dollar. We are told that hockey games would not draw the same gate if there were not a little violence taking place on the ice. That is quite cynical.
As long as the country wants to live by violence, some people in this country will die by violence. We will not end those deaths from occuring just by being violent toward the killers, because we have in fact been contributing to the killing by the way we let these patterns of profiting by violence by action or inaction, as in the case of industrial accidents, grow unchecked in our country.
There is no good reason for trying to blame it all on individuals who have committed murder. Therefore, I would not be able to support second reading of this Bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on seeing this Bill before the House, I am somewhat surprised because 1 realize that this is partly due to the Progressive Conservatives. At present they claim they are for the death penalty, but actually they are against something, they are against abolition because, they are against anything which exists, anything that is valid in our society. This will give me an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to quote from the official Record of Hansard of December, 1983, when the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) rose, this is on page 46 of Hansard, and asked where the Progressive Conservatives were standing. Well, here is the sponsor of the Bill who is always proud to launch crusades for or against something. Today, the only positive thing that can be noted, is that in the title of his Bill, he is in support of something because, actually, he is against it. That Hon. Member! He is against metric, as is his Party. He is against everything, against abolition. And, if I quote from Hansard on page 47, as suggested by the Right Hon. Prime Minister, when the more negative elements of reaction look for a place to go, they inevitably flock to the Progressive Conservative Party. It is the Party of those who are against. All those who say no when everybody else says yes, all those who are in favour of negativism, you can find them there, in the Opposition, Mr. Speaker. This is why we can draw an exhaustive list of them. We only have to dig in our memory, to remember those who
are against bilingualism, against unemployment insurance, against the changes in the Crow rate, against helping Cana-dair, against Bell Helicopterestablishing a plant in Quebec, against bilingualism in Manitoba. That is the Progressive Conservative Party. Today, the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) supports something; but what he supports is capital punishment, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, the only positive aspect of the matter is that, for once he is "for" something, despite that positive "for", he is against abolition of the death penalty. When the Right Hon. Prime Minister, at that time, and this is again taken from December 9, was referring to those who had not yet reached the current century, he meant the Progressive Conservatives. And this is where the previous speaker said: "You killed me, I am going to kill you. You did this, I am going to strike you. You slapped me in the face, I will slap you. Well, through that Bill, you killed, I am going to kill you."
Mr. Speaker, in 1976, this House voted the death penalty out of the books, yet the Official Opposition Party has not forgotten it. I remember that as recently as 1982, when the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) was leading the Official Opposition, there was an opposition day on that subject. I recall that the then leader of the Official Opposition, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead, was beyond himself, suggesting he was not supporting the reinstatement of capital punishment, but various things had to be considered and studies made. Although this is always a situation that has to be monitored, my view is that there was a vote here in this House in 1976. The penalties in the Criminal Code were changed to life emprisonment. When there is reference in the amending bill, through Clause 1 of the bill, for instance . . . Section 47 of the Criminal Code deals with high treason offences. What is the present wording of subsection 47(1) of the Criminal Code? Everyone-and besides, my colleague from Levis (Mr. Gourde) agrees with me, and I wish to congratulate him on his recent appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General. He will surely see to it that all those questions are debated and this one in particular, but today he may not have the opportunity to tell his constituents whether he supports capital punishment or not. However, he surely has a lot to say on the matter and he will deal with it in detail at a later date. Therefore, Subsection 47(1) at present reads as follows: Everyone who commits high treason is guilty of an indictable offence and shall be sentenced to imprisonment for life. Then, Subsection 47(4) at present reads as follows: For the purposes of Part XX, the sentence of imprisonment for life prescribed by subsection (1) is a minimum punishment, Mr. Speaker. Of course, first degree murder is also mentioned, under Section 218 of the present Criminal Code. Having practised law and as a practising lawyer from time to time, Mr. Speaker, when faced with this situation at the present stage of development of our society, one must look at reality with a view to improving things instead of remaining at a standstill as the Progressive Conservative Party wants to do. We must do one thing, namely
March 8, 1984

try to improve our social programs in order to help people who are in a depressive state, in financial difficulty or otherwise, and tend sometimes to be aggressive or too harsh with their fellow citizens. We must try to implement social programs but not at the expense of society by spending huge amounts of money to improve the social conditions of our fellow citizens, but in order to prevent violence. This is in contrast with the maxim I quoted at the beginning of my remarks: Thou hath killed, I will kill thee . . . Will that solve in anyway our society's problems? This maxim comes to my mind and I cannot help repeating it when I read the bill before us. In fact, since capital punishment was abolished, statistics do not point to an increase in violent crimes. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 45 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-DEVELOPMENT OF HIGH-TECH INDUSTRY- MONTREAL REGION
INDUSTRY-DEVELOPMENT OF HIGH-TECH INDUSTRY- MONTREAL REGION
speechtext:
In the 1980s and the 1990s, some high technology companies will be looking for locations giving them the opportunity to control their operating costs, to improve their productivity and maintain a fast pace of technological and product development. An important consultant firm for the establishment of companies, Fantus has recently made an analysis and a detailed assessment of the Montreal area to determine to what extent it would offer special advantages as a site for various kinds of high technology centres.
That report indicates that the choice of Montreal has substantial advantages for high technology. The table on page 6 clearly shows the advantages of that area as far as costs are concerned. Some annual savings of 37 to 51 per cent can be made in the region in comparison with other large metropolitan areas in the United States such as Boston, New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Chicago and the savings according to the size of the plants considered could vary between $8 and $11 million.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on February 8, I informed the House of the situation and of the contents of the report in a statement under Standing Order 21 and I asked the minister during the question period whether he had contacted his Quebec counterpart about this report because of the numerous advantages mentioned about Montreal. There is an ample source of electricity, a substantial pool of technical engineers and
Adjournment Debate
scientific personnel, a network of 20 CEGEPs in the metropolitan area of Montreal have turned out some 12,300 graduates in 1982 and finally, the seven engineering schools actively involved in research produced 2,100 graduates in 1982-83. The aerospace centres are also mentioned.
On the basis of those advantages Montreal seemed to be the ideal place to establish high technology plants. However, during consultations with several other companies mention was made of the limited nature of these advantages. How come? Well, management in the Province of Quebec, was too heavily taxed and Bill 17 created some political uncertainty. That was another constraint that made those advantages less appealing.
Mr. Speaker, when we hear Minister Gilbert Paquette speak of separatism, of independence and of sovereignty for Quebec, can we really say that such comments contribute to the establishment of Montreal as a aeronautical centre? Do they really help create jobs for our young people looking for one or is it not rather the way of mortgaging the future of thousands of Quebecers?
Therefore, I would ask, Mr. Speaker, and this is the reason why I took part in the debate this evening ... I think that we cannot overlook the tremendous advantages the city of Montreal has to offer, and I am proud of being part of a Government which over the last ten months has invested $2 billion in high technology in the Montreal area.
Therefore, I would ask the Minister not only to send the report to his Quebec counterpart, as he mentioned in his answer to me, but also to meet with Mr. Paquette in an effort to show him the district advantages offered by Montreal where young people would have extraordinary opportunities to find jobs in the field of high technology and where they could be assured of a good future rather than signing away their future as a result of his separatist attitude.
Therefore, I ask the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston), through his Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Dion), to request a meeting with Mr. Paquette in order to discuss this report and to consider seriously the best ways to encourage high technology industries to settle in Montreal.
