speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased, on behalf of the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology, to reply to the concerns of the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy) who, incidentally, is working very hard for the economic development of the Montreal area.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Lumley) has commissioned a report called the FANTUS report on the advantages of the Montreal area with regard to the establishment of high technology

March 8, 1984
Adjournment Debate
facilities. This report confirms that Montreal is a very attractive location for such investments and even provides many advantages as compared with many cities in the United States. More specifically, the area has several excellent technical colleges and universities in both English and French languages, something few North American cities can boast of.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are major assets to ensure the future industrial growth of Montreal as well as the diversification of the Quebec economy in general.
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to the Hon. Member for Laval that the federal government is fully confident in the potential of Montreal; this is reflected in the major investments in science and technology announced by this government over these last few months. The global value of those facilities exceeds SI 10 million to this day, and as was mentioned by the Hon. Member, the future investments in science and technology over the next few years will reach over $2.1 billion. The Office automation Centre in Laval, the Bell's Helicopter Plant, the Robotic Training Center in Sainte-Therese, the Food Processing Center in Saint-Hyacinthe, although only a few miles from Montreal, and the expansion of the Pulp and Paper Institute are some of the capital investment projects of the federal government. This demonstrates a genuine government concern for investments in the Montreal area.
The Hon. Member asked if the minister mentioned them to his Quebec counterpart. He told me personally, although the report is available to both levels of government, that he would certainly discuss the matter not only with the minister responsible for Science and Technology but also with all Quebec ministers who are again campaigning on the independence platform for the next provincial election. Their statements are of public record and they can only bring uncertainty once again to Quebec and to the Montreal area. And we have to dispel that uncertainty to be able to attract investments in Quebec and the rest of Canada. I will most certainly communicate the representations made by the Hon. Member for Laval to the Hon. Minister who will inform the Quebec government accordingly.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-REQUEST FOR INTERPRETATION OF SECTION 23(3)(B) OF CHARTER OF RIGHTS
THE CONSTITUTION-REQUEST FOR INTERPRETATION OF SECTION 23(3)(B) OF CHARTER OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to the debate this evening follows a numbers of questions I put to the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) on January 20 and January 27 of this year. Briefly, I was seeking to establish as clearly as possible the position of the federal Government on the interpretation of Section 23(6) of the Canadian Constitution of 1982, and more specifically, what this section means for Ontario, and I would refer my hon. colleagues to Hansard of January 23 of this year, when in a
debate similar to the one being held this evening, I said that in my opinion, Section 23(3)(6) gave the linguistic minority of a province the right to manage and control its educational institutions.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that last year, the Province of Ontario asked its highest court, the Ontario Court of Appeal, to rule on four questions. These four questions may be found in Order in Council 2154-83-Ontario, and I would invite my colleagues to read them if they are interested.
Among other things, the Court of Appeal was asked to rule on the matter of control and management by minorities of their educational institutions. The Court heard testimony in the middle of January of this year.
Intervenors included the federal Government, of course, which, in a well-prepared statement, unreservedly supported the position of the minorities, that is, that Section 23(3)(6) could be interpreted as giving a minority a constitutional right to control and manage the institutions in question or, if you prefer the constitutional term, its educational institutions.
It will be recalled that in his testimony, Federal Government counsel Brad Smith had expressed some doubt about management and control. He had stated, at least according to certain press reports, and I quote one of them: "The Canadian Constitution does not give minorities the right to manage and control their educational institutions". And again, according to Mr. Smith: "Management and control if necessary, but not necessarily management and control".
The press report goes on to say that Mr. Smith had maintained that the right to education in the language of the minority as guaranteed in the Constitution does not include the management and control of educational institutions.
That is the intervention which prompted me to ask the Minister of Justice to take a stand in the House on January 20.
I do not blame him, he supported his counsel by saying: "The Canadian Constitution does not guarantee to minority groups the right to control their educational institutions".
The media, newspapers, TV and radio, reported freely the remarks of the Attorney General and Minister of Justice, so much so that it has become a highly politicized issue with us, and people were wondering just what the federal Government position was on this question. Although the brief on the case tabled before the judges was clear and accurate enough, the interpretation given was not quite what was expected.
I think it might be appropriate as well to remind Hon. Members that, last January 27, I again put a question to the Minister and asked him to set the record straight and perhaps repeat or give us his interpretation. He stated, in a clear enough answer, clearer than the others, in my opinion: "Should a province decide to share its authority over education with its residents, it would then be under the obligation to
March 8, 1984

ensure equal treatment of the majority and minority groups in the province".
That, Mr. Speaker, is the essence of the federal argument. In other words, when a province has exclusive jurisdiction such as it has over education, but decides to share it with its residents, it must do so equitably with all residents, be they majority or minority groups. That has been the basic argument of minority groups for many years. Mr. Speaker, there is no question of invading a provincial jurisdiction. We are saying: Indeed, the province has exclusive jurisdiction, but if it does share it with its residents, it must do so equitably. A province which established school boards, for example, must establish school boards which take Section 93 into consideration, including religious denominations, as well as Section 23 of the Constitution Act, 1982, that is to say minority language educational rights. It must do so equitably.
I asked the Minister-and again I do so in concluding, Mr. Speaker, because my time is running out-to present, because of the perceptions, additional submissions to the courts. I realize that it is seldom done, that it is unusual. Still I thought it was necessary, considering that people feel that the federal Government was in fact quite ambiguous and hardly convincing on this question.
The Minister replied vaguely in the House that it might be something which he would take under consideration. I wrote to the Prime Minister to seek his support. I saw the Ministers whom I believed were involved in this matter. I am now asking the Parliamentary Secretary to tell me whether the federal Government has decided to present additional submissions to the courts in order to clear up this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Al MacBain (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-REQUEST FOR INTERPRETATION OF SECTION 23(3)(B) OF CHARTER OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is raising a very important question concerning the federal position on minority language education rights and, more specifically, on the interpretation to be given to Section 23(3)(Jb) of the Charter, insofar as it may relate to the management and control of minority language educational facilities by the linguistic minority of a province. He is also asking whether the Attorney General of Canada intends to present additional submissions to the Ontario Court of Appeal on this matter.
The Hon. Member is probably already aware that, on Tuesday, March 6, counsel for the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. MacGuigan) asked the Registrar of the Ontario Court of Appeal to inquire whether the court would be prepared to entertain a motion to permit the Attorney General of Canada to add to the submissions originally made on his behalf in the Ontario language reference which was heard last January and referred to by the Hon. Member. We are waiting for an answer from the court to that inquiry.
Adjournment Debate
In these circumstances, the Hon. Member will no doubt understand that it would be highly inappropriate to discuss in this House the reasons for which the Attorney General is asking the court to entertain the motion. Such reasons would have to be submitted to the court itself if it accepts to hear the motion. Morever, for the same reason, it would be totally inappropriate for me to outline here the nature of the additional submissions that would be made on behalf of the Attorney General of Canada, if it was decided by the Court of Appeal to entertain and to grant a hearing on the motion. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier will understand that such additional submissions would first have to be made to the court itself. I strongly believe that, having regard to the circumstances, with deference for the Court of Appeal, we ought to refrain from discussing this matter for the moment.
Having said that, however, I feel it is open to me to reaffirm the Government's position on Section 23. That section confers rights which are of fundamental importance to Canadians and to the nature of Canada as a bilingual country. There should therefore be no doubt about the approach of the Government to the interpretation of the section. It is our view that Section 23 (3) (b) in particular should be given a broad and liberal interpretation, a generous interpretation that is most consistent with the fullest realization of the minority language education rights which it entrenches and which lie at the very root of the future of bilingual Canada.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FARM FUEL SALES TAX. (B) THRONE SPEECH PROPOSAL TO HELP FARMERS
AGRICULTURE-FARM FUEL SALES TAX. (B) THRONE SPEECH PROPOSAL TO HELP FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would like to pursue the question I raised on March 5 regarding the problems faced by farmers. I would like to say that I am happy to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ferguson) here to answer the question. He has served on the Agricultural Committee so I think it is appropriate that the Department of Finance have the benefit of his expertise in that area. I am glad he will listen to the problem I raise here, because I was not satisfied with the answer I received from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
The Minister said that when the farming industry in Canada is compared to that of other industries, it is probably the best in the country. That particular response did not really strike any kind of soft chord in me, Mr. Speaker. All I have to do is look at the statistics we have with regard to the farm income situation in 1983, and the outlook for 1984. I refer the figures of the agricultural statistics division of Statistics Canada. The prediction for Manitoba is that we can expect a 26 per cent decline in realized net income for 1984. That is a rather bleak outlook in contrast to the rosy picture the Minister of Agriculture was painting.
I just want to emphasize how important it is that there be some sort of triggering of the mechanism with regard to the western grain stabilization fund, that there be some payouts

March 8, 1984
Adjournment Debate
immediately, because many of the farmers are in dire straits. I could elaborate further in respect to the farm incomes to which the Minister of Agriculture referred. He should be aware that the projected net farm income for 1984 is actually lower than the 1973 net farm income. In terms of actual dollars, the actual net farm income for Manitoba for 1984 is projected to be some $244 million and in 1973, it was $278 million. A lot of things have taken place between 1973 and 1984 and this certainly is not a bright picture.
On the other hand, if we were to look at the projected net income in terms of 1971 constant dollars-and again these are statistics from the agricultural division of Statistics Canada- we find that projected in 1971 constant dollars net farm income for farmers in Manitoba is $83 million for 1984, and it was $296 million in 1974. So we are talking about something projected for 1984 to be roughly between a quarter and a third of the 1974 net farm income for Manitoba.
I am trying to emphasize this critical situation, Mr. Speaker, so that the Minister of Agriculture will understand. Hopefully, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ferguson) will communicate this to him; that these rising costs are really hurting the farmers. If we look historically at why this has happened we find that the number one increase in costs to farmers in Manitoba-and farmers in my riding come into my office and show me their bank books and their income tax statements-is in fuel and fertilizers. These costs are becoming the number one costs farmers are faced with. It is because of this that I have been asking the Government to consider giving an energy rebate to farmers who are using diesel fuel and, of course, gasoline.
The excise tax which is rebated now, I am told by individual farmers, is of some help, but the excise tax does not apply, of course, to diesel fuels. More and more farmers are using diesel equipment on their farms and, therefore, we need some sort of rebate of sales tax. Of course, this sales tax would apply to gasoline and diesel fuel. I believe that the Government has room to manoeuvre in this regard, if it looks at the breakdown of the sales tax and, of course, other federal taxes which are involved there. These are things which could be done immediately to assist the farmer.
As far as the western grain stabilization plan is concerned, we had promises in the Speech from the Throne of changes, but I was a bit baffled as to why there was nothing in the Budget which would show that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is at least working on this particular problem. Hopefully today the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance will give me some good news which I can immediately pass on to the people in constituencies such as Dauphin-Swan River.
Discontent with the western grain stabilization plan is pretty well universal out west. There is a need for something to be done there and I suggest the Government consider making a pay-out retroactive to 1983 immediately so that farmers have money in their pockets to finance their seeding. It might also
consider combining any sort of new grain stabilization idea with something along the model of crop insurance, making it available on an individual basis to insure against crop fluctuations. I will eagerly await the Parliamentary Secretary's comments. I hope he has some good news for the farmers in western Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FARM FUEL SALES TAX. (B) THRONE SPEECH PROPOSAL TO HELP FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his comments. I have been following the situation very closely and I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said a few days ago that the Western Grain Stabilization Act is under review. However, we have to realize that wheat and grain prices reflect world market conditions.
Perhaps it sounds old hat, but for other commodities we grow, not only in western Canada but in eastern Canada, there are vehicles and legislation in place whereby farmers can organize to ensure that they have an income from the marketplace commensurate with that of the rest of society. I am speaking here of the poultry and dairy industries which have an excellent system of marketing in place, perhaps the envy of the world.
I fully realize that there is a special problem regarding grain markets which are depressed at the present time and we trust they will pick up and that this will be reflected in farm income.
The Hon. Member also raised an issue debated in this House on February 17, 1984, specifically that the federal Government provide a further subsidy for Canadian farmers by eliminating the 9 per cent federal sales tax on diesel fuel and gasoline used by farmers. At that time the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) proposed that the subject matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for consideration. Subsequently, with some wording changes, the House approved referral of the issue to the committee.
During that exchange of views it was pointed out that exempting gasoline and diesel fuel from sales tax for farmers, hunters, trappers and fishermen would present problems in ensuring that only those persons benefited from the relief, and denying it to others who would like to get on the tax free bandwagon. I should point out that the federal sales tax represents only a small portion of the price of a litre of fuel, less than 3 cents, and all users of motor fuels, including individuals, transportation companies, municipalities and manufacturers, in addition to farmers, are required to pay the tax.
However, it is important to look at what has been done for farmers in the recent Budget. There are proposals to shelter up to $120,000 in capital gains by placing them in RRSPs. Incorporated farmers and fishermen will benefit from the new proposals which will simplify the law for small incorporated firms. The Budget went a long way to accommodating the concerns of farmers, and I hope the committee will seriously consider the pros and cons of a sales tax concession for farm
March 8, 1984

fuels, as the Government is well aware of the needs and concerns of the agricultural community.
